title: Sin Crouches at the Door — Offering, Door, Mark
blocks: Brothers and sisters, last time we stopped at a garment: God made coats of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them, and then sent them out of the garden of Eden. Today we look at the first generation born outside the garden.

And the question of this chapter is one you and I may have met just this week. Have you ever had that moment when you see someone else praised, chosen, blessed — and something in you sinks? Your mouth says congratulations, and then you get home and cannot settle no matter how you turn it over.

Let me give you the answer up front: envy never stays inside. It always walks as far as the door. And God came and gave his warning before anything happened — the question was never whether you have feelings. The question is whether you listen to the sentence he says at the door.

Verse 1: "The man knew Eve his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Cain." That word "knew" is יָדַע (*yada*), the same "know" as in "knowing good and evil" from the last lesson. The deepest kind of knowing, used of a husband and wife.

When Eve gives birth to Cain she says, "I have gotten a man with Yahweh's help." She names him Cain, a name close in sound to "gotten". The second son is called Abel, in Hebrew הֶבֶל (*Hevel*) — the very word translated "vanity" in Ecclesiastes, and meaning literally "a breath." Brothers and sisters, the text records nothing his mother said at his birth. One name means "gotten"; the other means "a breath." From the very first line the author is laying the weight of this chapter in place.

Verses 3 and 4: "As time passed, Cain brought an offering to Yahweh from the fruit of the ground. Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat." Compare the wording carefully. Cain brings "from the fruit of the ground" — with no adjective at all. Abel brings "the firstborn of his flock and of its fat" — מִבְּכֹרוֹת (*mibechorot*), the first portion; and the fat, the best part.

Then verses 4 and 5 say, "Yahweh respected Abel and his offering, but he didn't respect Cain and his offering." Notice the order: the person first, the offering second. God looks at the man before he looks at what is in the man's hands. Hebrews 11:4 makes it plainer still: "By faith, Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain."

Brothers and sisters, we must be careful here. This passage is not saying that God prefers meat to vegetables — the grain offering in Leviticus is equally acceptable to God. The difference is not in the kind of offering but in whether the one offering it has given God the best and the first. Is what you gave this week your surplus, or your firstborn? Is the time you give God your sharpest stretch of the day, or the ten minutes left over after you have finished scrolling?
Why did God respect Abel's offering and not Cain's? Isn't that favouritism?

The text does not state the reason outright, so we must speak from the clues Scripture gives elsewhere rather than from imagination. Hebrews 11:4 says, "By faith, Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain." The weight falls on "by faith." And the wording of the text leaves a clue of its own: Abel brought "the firstborn of his flock and of its fat" — the first and the best; Cain's is described only as "from the fruit of the ground", with nothing said about firstfruits. So the difference very likely lies not in the kind of gift but in the direction of the heart. That is intensely practical for us: what God looks at is not what we produce, but where he ranks in our thinking at the moment we produce it.
2. God Walks Over and Speaks to the One Who Was Refused
The second half of verse 5: "Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell." The Hebrew is vivid: his face *fell down*.
Then in verse 6 God does something that astonishes me every time I read it: he walks over and talks to him. "Yahweh said to Cain, 'Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen?'"

Brothers and sisters, stop here. Cain is the one who has been refused, and God does not turn and walk away, nor does he begin with a rebuke. He approaches an angry man with two questions. And notice what God asks — *why*. He wants Cain to look inside himself.

Many people have been wounded in ministry and feel that God plays favourites: why was he chosen and not me? This chapter's answer is not an explanation but an action — God walks over to the man who was not chosen and speaks to him. The one who was refused turns out to be the one who receives God's personal counsel.

Verse 7 is the centre of the chapter, and the verse I would ask everyone to commit to memory: "If you do well, won't it be lifted up? If you don't do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it."
If God knew Cain was going to strike, why did he not simply stop him?

God did in fact intervene — he walked over and spoke to him in person, and he put it very plainly: "If you do well, won't it be lifted up? If you don't do well, sin crouches at the door." That is both a warning and an invitation. But God did not take away his freedom. The most moving thing about this verse is this: God speaks to a man in the middle of his anger, and his tone is gentle. He asks, "Why are you angry?" and only then does he set out the principle. So what we have to learn is not merely "do not sin" but also "how to speak to a person who is angry" — ask what happened first, and give the principle afterwards. As for why God does not compel people, the tree in chapter 3 has already answered that: without freedom there is no love.
3. A Light from the Original: a Beast Crouching at the Door
There are three words in this verse we must see clearly.

The first is "do well", תֵּיטִיב (*teitiv*). Notice that this is a conditional clause, not a verdict. God says, "If you … then …". Which is to say: the door is still open. God is not announcing that Cain is finished. God is telling him that he still has a choice.

The second word is "crouches", רֹבֵץ (*rovets*). It means to lie in wait — the posture of a beast hunkered down, body low, ready to spring. So the picture God gives is this: there is an animal crouching at your door. It is not inside you; it is outside. It has not come in yet, but it is waiting.

The third word is "desire", תְּשׁוּקָה (*teshuqah*). The last time this word appeared was Genesis 3:16, "your desire will be for your husband." Here its sense is far clearer: it wants to master you. So the tone of that sentence in 3:16 is explained for us by this verse — it describes a tug of war over power, not a sweet attachment.

And God finishes: "but you are to rule over it." Brothers and sisters, that is a command, and it is also a guarantee. God does not command what he will not give you the power to do. Sin crouches at the door, but the door handle is on your side.

Note especially when this happens: God's warning comes *before* the murder, not after. The anger inside you that has not yet acted — that, right now, is the door. The most important thing you can do this week is to shut that door while you still think there is time.
"Sin crouches at the door" — doesn't picturing sin as a wild animal give people an excuse to duck responsibility?

Quite the reverse: the very next clause puts the responsibility back on the person — "Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it." "Desire" and "rule" here are the same pair of words God used to the woman in 3:16 — a relationship of struggle. So what the image says is this: sin has real power; it crouches, it waits, it springs. But it is not the master. You are. That cuts two ways in practice. On one side, do not underestimate it and imagine willpower will do. On the other, do not deify it and turn "I couldn't help it" into a disclaimer. The real way out is what the New Testament says — through him who strengthens us, and not facing it alone. Let somebody know what is crouching at your door.
Verse 8: "Cain said to Abel, his brother, 'Let's go into the field.' While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him."

At this point the Hebrew Masoretic text contains the most famous blank in the chapter: "Cain said to Abel, his brother" — and what he said is not written. Some ancient versions supply "let us go into the field." But the Masoretic text simply leaves the gap. Brothers and sisters, that blank is frightening: he spoke to his brother, and what he said does not matter. What matters is that while he was speaking, he had already decided.
And here is a detail worth counting: the word "brother" occurs seven times in this chapter. The author keeps reminding you — that is his brother, that is his brother, that is his brother.

Then verse 9: "Yahweh said to Cain, 'Where is Abel, your brother?'" אֵי (*ei*), where. Brothers and sisters, this is the second "where" God asks. In chapter 3 he asks Adam, "Where are you?"; in chapter 4 he asks Cain, "Where is your brother?" Put the two questions together and you have the two great commandments of the whole Bible: your relationship with God, and your relationship with people.

Cain's answer is the most famous piece of insolence in Scripture: "I don't know. Am I my brother's keeper?" That word "keeper" is שֹׁמֵר (*shomer*) — precisely the commission God gave humanity in Genesis 2:15, "to cultivate and keep it." Brothers and sisters, the thing he throws back at God is exactly the thing God had entrusted to him.

God says, "The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground." The blood of a victim speaks. And Hebrews 12:24 says that the sprinkled blood of Jesus "speaks better than that of Abel." Two lots of blood spilled on the ground: one cries out for justice, the other cries out forgiveness.
Is "Where is your brother?" the same kind of question as "Where are you?" in chapter 3?

It is the same kind, and it takes a step further. In chapter 3 God asks a person, "Where are you?", dealing with our relationship with God; in chapter 4 he asks, "Where is Abel, your brother?", dealing with our relationship with each other. Setting the two questions side by side, Scripture is saying: once the relationship with God has broken, the next thing to break will be the relationship with people. And Cain's answer, "Am I my brother's keeper?", uses the very verb (שָׁמַר) used in chapter 2 for keeping the garden. The commission God gave humanity was always to keep — to keep the garden, and to keep the people beside us. So his retort was a refusal, to God's face, of the very office God had given him.
Cain committed murder and God gave him a protective mark. Is that fair?

This verse is not describing indulgence; it is describing God breaking the cycle of blood vengeance. Cain says, "Whoever finds me will kill me", and the mark God gives cuts the chain of retaliation — it stops one killing from becoming a clan feud. And God does not waive the consequences: Cain is cursed, driven from the soil he tilled, and becomes a fugitive and a wanderer. So justice and mercy are both present here at once. This verse runs on into Romans 12, "don't seek revenge yourselves", and on to the cross — where the blood of the one truly innocent man did not cry for retribution but said, "Father, forgive them." That is exactly what Hebrews 12 means when it says the blood of Jesus "speaks better than that of Abel."
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is saying God plays favourites. Some finish this chapter concluding that God simply liked Abel better. But Hebrews states plainly that Abel offered "by faith", and the order in the text is "respected Abel and his offering" — the person first. More importantly, God did not abandon Cain; he walked over and talked to him. When you have finished this section, your congregation's impression of God should be that he is just, not that he is capricious.

The second is putting the whole difference down to blood sacrifice versus grain offering. That is the easiest way to preach it, and it misleads people into thinking ritual settles everything — get the item right and God is obliged to accept. What God says in verse 7 is "if you do well"; the weight is on the heart and the conduct. The grain offering in Leviticus is equally acceptable.

The third is preaching Cain's mark as the brand of a curse. Verse 15 says plainly that the mark was to keep him from being killed. It is grace. There have been people in history who twisted it into a matter of skin colour and ethnicity to prop up slavery — the text contains no such suggestion whatsoever, and that is a thorough abuse of it. When you speak of that mark, your congregation should feel protection, not humiliation.

The fourth is preaching that envy can be solved simply by "praising others more." Verse 7 says sin is a beast crouched and waiting to spring. That is something to be dealt with, not something to be papered over with positive thinking. Change only the vocabulary and leave the root, and the feeling will come back — and it will be bigger next time.

The fifth is treating the Lamech section as a hymn to the progress of civilisation. Verses 20 to 22 do record the building of cities, herding, the harp, the forging of bronze and iron — and those abilities are themselves God's gift to humanity. But the author has deliberately placed in the middle of that same section the first poem in the Bible, and it is a poem boasting of a killing. As technology climbs, violence climbs with it. Preach only the first half and you miss what the author is actually doing.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: the most wounding thing in Chinese families is comparison — grades, jobs, children, who is the more filial. What does this chapter say about that? Brothers and sisters, this chapter begins with an act of comparison and ends with a human life. So Scripture takes comparison extremely seriously; it is not harmless family entertainment. But let me point out something important: what God said to Cain was not "stop comparing yourself with your brother." What he said was, "If you do well, won't it be lifted up?" That is, the way out is not to tell him to stop caring; it is to move his eyes off his brother and back onto God. That distinction is very practical: tell someone who has been compared all his life to "stop caring" and he cannot do it — but if he genuinely knows how he is regarded in God's sight, the comparison loses its weight of itself.

The second question: elders often say that harmony in the home makes everything prosper, so when something serious happens in the family it should be pressed down and not spoken of. Is that right? My answer is that this chapter gives a very severe reply: blood speaks. Verse 10 says, "The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground." What has been pressed down does not disappear; it makes a sound out of the ground. Brothers and sisters, covering up and forgiving are two different things. Forgiveness brings the matter into the light, deals with it, and then puts it down. Covering up pretends it never happened. Real harmony is not that nobody speaks; it is that after it has been spoken through, people can still sit down together. If there is something in your family that has gone unaddressed for years, this verse is for you: God can hear that sound.
When I see someone else blessed and it makes me uncomfortable, how do I handle that kind of envy?

Start by acknowledging its weight, exactly as the text does: Cain's murder did not begin with hatred, it began with a face falling. So the first step is neither to dismiss that small discomfort nor to pretend it is not there — God asks, "Why are you angry?", and he allows a person to put the feeling into words. The second step is to find the thought underneath it: beneath envy there is usually a sentence such as "what he has should have been mine." The third step is hard and highly effective: bless that person concretely, by name, asking God to give him double. The first time you do it, it will stick in your throat; do it for a while and the cord loosens. If the envy has been building for years and is affecting your sleep and your relationships, find a pastor or professional help; do not carry it alone.
7. Living 321 Out — Hand Sovereignty Over at the Door
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Abel's blood cries out from the ground, and the blood of the Lord Jesus speaks better than the blood of Abel. One cries for justice; the other cries forgiveness. So my example is very concrete: when I am wronged, ask for forgiveness before asking for justice. That is not telling you to pretend it does not hurt. It is saying that you may hand the justice over to the God who can hear the voice of blood.

The Bible is my standard — the standard in this chapter is extremely concrete: verse 7. It gives us a line to judge by: the feeling is not the sin; opening the door is. You may be angry — Ephesians 4:26 says, "Be angry, and don't sin" — but you must know that the beast is crouching there. The standard does not require you to have no feelings. It teaches you to recognise where the line runs.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice that God came before Cain acted. The Holy Spirit's work is often just like that today: in the three seconds before you press send, something inside says "don't". That voice is the warning at the door. Whether you listen decides everything that follows.

Let Jesus be King — "but you are to rule over it." God puts the responsibility into human hands; the door handle is on my side. So letting Jesus be King means handing sovereignty over in the thirty seconds when the feeling surges — handing it not to the anger, but to him. Brothers and sisters, the real spiritual battle mostly happens inside those thirty seconds.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — there is something in this chapter that is very easy to read past: after Cain has killed, God does not kick him aside. God sets a mark to protect him. Even inside the judgement, God is still protecting. The glory goes to him not only because he is just, but because he is merciful at the point where a person deserves it least.

Establish God's system — the end of chapter 4 says, "At that time men began to call on Yahweh's name." While Cain was building his city, while civilisation was expanding and Lamech was boasting, another line quietly began. Brothers and sisters, establishing God's system usually does not happen on the noisiest side; it happens among the small group who are willing to call on his name. Your group is small — that is all right. The brightest sentence in chapter 4 sits right beside its darkest page.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We talk a great deal about selflessness, and this chapter reminds us that selflessness does not mean having no feelings. God did not rebuke Cain for having a feeling; what he asked was, "Why are you angry?" A church that believes being spiritual means you may not be sad, may not be angry, may not say it out loud, will end up producing a room full of people with a beast shut inside them. The right road is not to hide the feeling but to bring the feeling to God and say it plainly — and then make the decision at the door.
"Deal with the heart before you deal with the matter" — but some things are urgent. What if there is no time to deal with the heart?

Urgent things must of course be handled; the text is not telling anyone to leave work undone. But notice the time lag in Cain's story: his face fell first, and only later were the two of them "in the field." There was time in between. In practice: do the work, but give yourself thirty seconds before you act — check whether you are solving the problem or evening the score. Those thirty seconds are the most practical shape of "ruling over it." Another useful boundary: do not press send at the peak of the feeling, and do not answer that message late at night. What is urgent is usually the task, not the heart; and what people get wrong is usually not the urgent task but the unprocessed anger inside it.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Crouching Beast
Brothers and sisters, the same sentence — "sin crouches at the door" — produces four completely different reactions in four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "This chapter is about people like Cain, not about me." Brothers and sisters, notice that Cain was not an atheist. He brought an offering, he knew who God was, and God spoke to him personally. He was a man with a religious life. 1 John 3:15 says, "Whoever hates his brother is a murderer." That verse drags the threshold right up to every one of our feet.

The fearful heart says, "That beast is far too strong; I could never hold it off." To that heart I say: read the verse to the end. God says sin crouches at the door, and then he says, "but you are to rule over it." God does not issue an order he will not give you the power to carry out. And 1 Corinthians 10:13 says God will make the way of escape. The door handle is on your side.

The ashamed heart says, "I opened that door long ago. It is too late." Brothers and sisters, look at verse 15. Cain had already struck; he had already killed. And what God gave him was a mark of protection. You will never be further beyond hope than the first murderer. God's mercy runs further than your failure.

The wounded heart says, "And what about me? I am the Abel here." There is one person in this chapter who never says a single word, and it is the one who was killed. Brothers and sisters, if you are the one who was wronged, the one who was pressed down, the one nobody spoke up for, hear verse 10: "The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground." You do not have to be loud. God can hear. Your case has not been overlooked. The day of accounting simply has not come yet.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, find your signal. Before anyone loses control of a feeling, the body gives a signal first — the voice speeds up, the breathing goes shallow, the fists close, or you fall suddenly silent. This week's assignment is to recognise it. To recognise the signal is to recognise that you are standing at the door.

Second, write down the person or the situation that most easily makes you envious, and admit it honestly. It need not be shown to anyone; write it for yourself and for God. The first thing God asked Cain was "why are you angry?" — he wants a person to say it himself.

Third, bless out loud, once, the person you find hardest to bless. Not thinking it in your head — actually saying it, even if only you and God hear. This is the most practical act there is for keeping the beast outside the door.
Fourth, do one act of keeping your brother. Go out of your way for someone you could perfectly well ignore. Cain said, "Am I my brother's keeper?", and God's answer is: yes, you are.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: Genesis 4 records humanity's first murder, and the cause was not hatred but envy; God came and warned him before he struck, saying that sin is like a beast crouching at the door — but the door handle is on your side; so I have learned that the question is not whether I have feelings, but whether I stop at the door.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that another person's blessing is not a verdict against me, and I will stop measuring myself by comparison.
I declare that when the feeling surges I will stop at the door, because the door handle is on my side.
I declare that I am my brother's keeper, because that is the commission God gave me in the first place.
I declare that when I am wronged I will ask first for forgiveness, and hand the justice to the God who hears.
This week I am supposed to "hear the person who has no voice" — but I have no idea who needs it.

Start with the circle closest to you, and do not go looking for a moving story. Three very practical clues. First, who has suddenly gone quiet lately — stopped speaking in the group chat, leaves quickly after the meeting? Second, who is most often talked about and least often asked after? Third, when whose name comes to mind do you feel a slight discomfort — that discomfort is usually a word you owe him. Once you have found the person, do not send a long speech; just ask, "How have you been? You came to mind." Abel's blood cried "to God" from the ground — God hears a great many voices we do not, and the reason we do not is that we have never come close enough to hear them.

Brothers and sisters, this chapter is heavy reading: an offering goes wrong, a brother is murdered, and violence escalates generation by generation until Lamech openly sings a song boasting of a killing and inflates God's sevenfold into a seventy-sevenfold of his own.
And yet the author leaves you a lamp in the last line. Verse 26: "At that time men began to call on Yahweh's name."

While Cain's line was building cities, expanding, escalating, Seth's line began doing something very small — they called on the name of God. No city, no instruments, no bronze or iron. Only prayer. And that line runs all the way to Abraham, to David, to Bethlehem.

And there is one more thing I want you to see. The Lord Jesus later said to Peter, "not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven." He used Lamech's number. The same figure: Lamech used it to reckon revenge, and the Lord Jesus used it to reckon forgiveness. Brothers and sisters, which set of books are you keeping today?

The focus is not on whether I was chosen, not on what somebody else received, and not on whether I have lost out again this time. The focus is on Jesus — his blood speaks better than the blood of Abel. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to stop at the door, to keep that beast outside, and to begin calling on his name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear conviction.
1. ★★ Hebrews says Abel offered "by faith". From the wording of this chapter, can you see where the difference between the two offerings lies?
2. ★★★ "Sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it." That sentence says two things at once. What are they? What goes wrong if you preach only one of them?
3. ★ The first thing God said to a man in the middle of his anger was, "Why are you angry?" What does that way of asking teach us?
4. ★★ "Am I my brother's keeper?" uses the same verb as "keeping" the garden in chapter 2. What is that coincidence saying?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I tried harder than he did; why him?), fearful (afraid of not being chosen), ashamed (what I bring is never good enough), wounded (someone has compared me with others). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "If you do well, won't it be lifted up?" Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ In the past six months, has someone's good news left you uncomfortable? You need not say the name. Only say this: underneath that discomfort, what was the sentence in your heart?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The matter in which I most easily feel that God plays favourites is …"
9. ★★ This week, for which person you once envied will you pray a concrete blessing? Say what you will ask God to give him.

Leader's reminder: questions five and seven touch feelings that are very hard to admit. The leader should go first with his own. If someone names a person inside the group as the object of his envy, do not adjudicate the rights and wrongs on the spot; follow up privately afterwards.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ "Where is your brother?" — in your home this week, is there someone you ought to go and see? Say his name and what you will do.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work, at school or in your group chats, who has suddenly gone quiet lately?

12. ★★★ The thirty-second practice: this week, every time the feeling rises and you are about to press send, stop for thirty seconds and ask, "Am I solving the problem or evening the score?" Say where you most often need those thirty seconds.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and tell him your answer to question seven this week. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, the Bible's first murder began with a man's face falling. Second, God walked over and spoke to him before it happened, and told him, "you are to rule over it." Third, so I have learned to stop for thirty seconds when the feeling rises. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the person you will go and see this week, and who you will tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that in days when a beast crouches at our door we would still be the one who keeps his brother.
